arXiv:2104.08050v3 [cs.PF] 17 Oct 2021

Age of information without service preemption

George Kesidis ††thanks: gik2@psu.edu; Univ. of Pennsylvania, USA    Takis Konstantopoulos ††thanks: takiskonst@gmail.com; Univ. of Liverpool, UK; research supported by Cast. Co. IIS-75    Michael A. Zazanis ††thanks: zazanis@aueb.gr; Athens Univ. of Economics and Business, Greece
Abstract

When designing a message transmission system, from the point of view of making sure that the information transmitted is as fresh as possible, two rules of thumb seem reasonable: use small buffers and adopt a last-in-first-out policy. In this paper, we measure freshness of information using the “age of information” performance measure. Considering it as a stochastic process operating in a stationary regime, we compute not just the first moment but the whole marginal distribution of the age of information (something important in applications) for two well-performing systems. In neither case do we allow for preemption of the message being processed because this may be difficult to implement in practice. We assume that the arrival process is Poisson and that the messages have independent sizes (service times) with common distribution. We use Palm and Markov-renewal theory to derive explicit results for Laplace transforms. In particular, this approach can be used to analyze more complex last-in-first-out systems with larger buffer sizes.

1 Introduction

Traditionally, networked systems performance is measured with respect to buffer sizes and delays. Relatively recently, there has been a shift in what is considered important both in terms of design and performance. The introduction of the so-called “age of information” (usually abbreviated as AoI), defined as the elapsed time since the information possessed by a monitor is generated and time stamped at the source, has received a lot of attention. The reason is simple: in several applications it is the freshness of information that is important rather than the correct transmission of all packets. Examples include virtual reality, online gaming, weather reports, autonomous driving, stock market trading, decision systems for an airplane, power systems, sensor/actuator systems and other other “cyber physical” systems.

We start by precisely defining the concept of AoI in general. Consider a message processing facility with one input stream of arriving messages. The facility can be a single queue or a complex network system. An arriving message has a certain positive “size” (expressed in time units and interpreted as processing or service time) and three things can happen: (i) the message is immediately rejected upon arrival; (ii) the message is accepted but rejected while in the system; (iii) the message is successfully transmitted as soon as it is processed in its entirety. We are interested in the time that the latter will happen in comparison to the time that the message arrives in the system. If messages are labeled by integers in a way that the message with label n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z} arrives at time Tn∈ℝT_{n}\in\mathbb{R} and Tm<TnT_{m}<T_{n} if m<nm<n, if Tn+ΔnT_{n}+\Delta_{n} denotes the time at which message labeled nn leaves the system either by being rejected or successfully transmitted, and if ψn\psi_{n} is a binary variable indicating the latter (ψn=1\psi_{n}=1 if message nn is successful or 00 if not), then we let

D⁡(t)\displaystyle D(t) :=sup{Tn+Δn:n∈ℤ,Tn+Δn≤t,ψn=1},\displaystyle:=\sup\{T_{n}+\Delta_{n}:\,n\in\mathbb{Z},T_{n}+\Delta_{n}\leq t,\psi_{n}=1\}, (1)
A⁡(t)\displaystyle A(t) :=sup{Tn:n∈ℤ,Tn+Δn≤t,ψn=1},\displaystyle:=\sup\{T_{n}:\,n\in\mathbb{Z},T_{n}+\Delta_{n}\leq t,\psi_{n}=1\}, (2)

and define the AoI at time tt by

α⁡(t):=t−A⁡(D⁡(t)).\alpha(t):=t-A(D(t)). (3)

Quite simply, D⁡(t)D(t) is the time of the last successful departure before tt and A⁡(D⁡(t))A(D(t)) is the arrival time of the message that departed at time D⁡(t)D(t). This definition is quite general, that is, it does not depend on the details of the system design.

Typically, systems that adopt freshness of information as performance measure should be designed so that its AoI “be as small as possible”. The last phrase can mean several things. For example, it can mean that the quantity α⁡(t)\alpha(t) is least for all tt under identical traffic conditions. Or it could mean least in terms of an expectation or another functional of the process. Adopting AoI as a performance criterion immediately poses some simplifications over traditional queueing theory performance criteria but also presents some new challenges.

Suppose that the processing facility is a queue with one server and buffer consisting of a finite or infinite number of cells. One of the cells of the buffer is occupied by the message being processed and the rest of the cells are occupied by stored messages. If we are free to design the buffer and the service policy as we wish, how do we do this if we wish to keep the AoI “as small as possible”?

It is reasonable to conjecture that every time a message arrives we process it immediately (after all, we are not interested in obsolete information.) That is, even if the server is busy at the moment of arrival, the currently served message is immediately discarded and the new one starts being processed. Systems working in this manner are service-preemptive. It also seems reasonable to serve messages in reverse order of arrival: the most recent message must be served first (LIFO).

One may thus conjecture that LIFO-preemptive (meaning: service preemptive) is “best”. But numerical examples and simulations show that this is false depending on the model assumptions. In particular, a single buffer system with no service preemption (called ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} below) has smaller AoI both in expectation and stochastically under particular assumptions on the message size distribution [14, 6, 10]. In fact, we conjectured in [10] that the so-called 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} system (see below and Figure 1 for the definition) has lower AoI than ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}. In this paper, inter alia, we resolve this issue.

The simplest systems with small-size buffer and no service preemption are defined next. One of them, denoted as ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}, is nothing else but a single-server queue with buffer of size 22 and blocking. That is, an incoming message finding the buffer full is immediately discarded. The other one, denoted as 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, also works without service preemption. An arriving message in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} finding the buffer full displaces or “pushes out” the stored message. See Figure 1 for a typical scenario in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}.

More generally, we define, for n≥2n\geq 2, ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} and 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} as follows. The ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} system is simply a single-server queue with buffer of size nn, operating under FIFO (First In First Out) policy and blocking of any incoming message finding the buffer full. The 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} system, for n≥2n\geq 2, works as follows: messages are stored in an order that is reverse to their order of arrival; so if there is a message being processed in cell 1 at time tt, the message in cell 2 arrived last before tt while the message in cell nn is the oldest; a new message arriving at a full buffer is always stored in cell 2, displacing the other messages upwards and pushing out the one sitting in cell nn (oldest one). For n≥2n\geq 2, 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} has no service preemption.

Note that in some cases, queuing and service policies may be subject to technological constraints (e.g., whether non-FIFO dequeueing or preemptive service policies are feasible, and what aspects of the queueing system are observable). In particular, ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} may be the best policy if LIFO dequeueing, queue pushout, and service preemption are all infeasible but blocking is, cf. Section 5.6.

For n=1n=1, the system ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} is simply a single-buffer blocking queue: an arriving message is immediately rejected if there is a message in the system. The 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} system is the single-buffer push-out system: an arriving message pushes out the currently processed message and takes its place. The 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} and ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} systems were analyzed under very general conditions in [6, 10].

Of all systems 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}, ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, the 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} system is special because it is the only one for which service preemption is allowed.

In this paper, we analyze the AoI processes and derive the stationary AoI distribution for the ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} (in Section 3) and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} (in Section 4) systems under a Poisson arrival process but generally distributed message sizes. The distribution for 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} case was previously derived in [6]. The technique used herein is different from that of [6, 10] and is easily generalizable to other systems, particularly to LIFO “dequeuing” policies 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} for n>2n>2 [11]. Indeed, we use the classical embedding technique, valid for queueing systems with Poisson arrivals (see, e.g. [4]), giving that the system sampled at certain epochs (the departures of successful messages in our case) has a Markovian property. This, of course, depends crucially on the Poisson property of the arrival process, so, for more general arrival processes (as in the case of [6, 10]) we need a different method that is substantially more complex and shall not be considered herein.

Under our assumptions, and because we consider finite buffers, it holds that there is a unique stationary version of the stochastic process α\alpha in all systems considered. We will not offer any reasons for this technical result, but only point out that even existence may not hold if the arrival and message size processes are neither independent nor renewal, and point out the difficulties by referring to [2]. We shall always be considering the stationary version. Hence α⁡(t)\alpha(t) has the same distribution for all tt. This is precisely what we are interested in describing. We note that computing the expectation is, in general, not that much easier than deriving the whole distribution. We also note that deriving the distribution is essential in case that we are interested not just in maintaining a low AoI on the average but also in maintaining the tail of the probability distribution small.

While our techniques are generalizable to all 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} and ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n}, for any positive integer nn, we only work with n=2n=2 for the following reason. We claim that the random variables α𝒫n​(t)\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}}(t), αℬn​(t)\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(t), n≥3n\geq 3, are stochastically larger than α𝒫n​(t)\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}}(t), αℬn​(t)\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(t), n∈{1,2}n\in\{1,2\}. Although, currently, we have no full proof of this fact, we have enough evidence to pose this as a conjecture. We partially prove and justify this conjecture in Section 5.6.

Throughout the paper, we let λ\lambda be the rate of the (Poisson) arrival process and GG the distribution of a typical message size σ\sigma, a random variable that is positive with probability 11 and has finite expectation denoted by 1/μ1/\mu. We thus only assume that λ>0\lambda>0 and μ>0\mu>0 (but σ\sigma may have infinite variance). It is assumed that the message sizes are i.i.d. copies of σ\sigma and independent of the arrival process. The ratio ρ=λ/μ\rho=\lambda/\mu is referred to as traffic intensity.

The main results of the paper are Theorems 1 and 2. We here present a special case. When the message sizes are i.i.d. exponential, having (for notational convenience) rate μ=1\mu=1, we shall show as a corollary that, in steady-state, the value of AoI at some (and hence any) point of time, has density

fℬ2​(t)\displaystyle f_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}(t) =c⁡(q⁡(t)​e−t+e−λ​t),\displaystyle=c\,(q(t)e^{-t}+e^{-\lambda t}), (4)
f𝒫2​(t)\displaystyle f_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(t) =q1​(t)​e−t+q2​(t)​e−(λ+1)​t−λλ−1​e−λ​t,\displaystyle=q_{1}(t)e^{-t}+q_{2}(t)e^{-(\lambda+1)t}-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-1}e^{-\lambda t}, (5)

in the 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} and ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} cases, respectively, where

c=λ(λ2+λ+1)​(λ−1)2,\displaystyle c=\frac{\lambda}{(\lambda^{2}+\lambda+1)(\lambda-1)^{2}}, q⁡(t)=12​λ​(λ−1)2​t2+λ⁡(λ−1)​t−1,\displaystyle\quad q(t)=\tfrac{1}{2}\lambda(\lambda-1)^{2}t^{2}+\lambda(\lambda-1)t-1,\quad
q1​(t)=(λ3+λ2−2​λ)​t−λ2+λ+3(λ2+λ+1)​(λ−1),\displaystyle q_{1}(t)=\frac{({\lambda}^{3}+{\lambda}^{2}-2\,\lambda)t-{\lambda}^{2}+\lambda+3}{(\lambda^{2}+\lambda+1)(\lambda-1)}, q2​(t)=(λ2+λ)​t+λ2+3​λ+3λ2+λ+1,\displaystyle\quad q_{2}(t)=\frac{({\lambda}^{2}+\lambda)t+{\lambda}^{2}+3\,\lambda+3}{\lambda^{2}+\lambda+1},

when λ≠1\lambda\neq 1; while, for λ=1\lambda=1, the densities become

fℬ2​(t)=13​(t2+t)​e−t,f𝒫2​(t)=13​(7+2​t)​e−2​t+13​(6​t−7)​e−t.f_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}(t)=\tfrac{1}{3}(t^{2}+t)e^{-t},\quad f_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(t)=\tfrac{1}{3}(7+2t)e^{-2t}+\tfrac{1}{3}(6t-7)e^{-t}.

(For general μ\mu, simply replace λ\lambda by λ/μ\lambda/\mu and tt by μ​t\mu t in the foregoing expressions.) These results are by themselves generalizations of what is already in the literature. For instance, in [14] the expectations for ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, see (33) and (23) in Corollaries 2 and 4 infra, have been computed under the same probabilistic assumptions. Notice that, in particular,

limλ→∞fℬ2​(t)=12​t2​e−t,limλ→∞f𝒫2​(t)=t​e−t,\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}f_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}(t)=\frac{1}{2}t^{2}e^{-t},\quad\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}f_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(t)=te^{-t},

and the limiting functions are probability densities as well. The first one is Erlang(3) and the second Erlang(2). Similar limits can be obtained for 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} and ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n}, without computations, simply by considering the system dynamics. In fact, we can interpret ℬ∞\mathcal{B}_{\infty} as a single server queue with infinite buffer operating under the FIFO discipline. From the point of view of AoI, this system is worst and should not be considered. Our practical rule of thumb says that one should store at most one message and discard everything beyond that, insofar as keeping AoI low is the goal. This rule of thumb may not be always optimal but it is frequently close to optimal.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We explain the basis of the technique used in Section 2 and see why it is absolutely general, as long as the system, possibly a network, has Poisson arrivals. The ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} system is considered in Section 3 and the 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} in Section 4. Section 5 contains a number of interesting observations. First it provides comparisons of the systems analyzed in this paper, together with the systems 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} and ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} (analyzed under more general assumptions in [6, 10]). Second, it explains what the limits of the AoI are when λ→∞\lambda\to\infty. Third, it gives a way to understand the AoI for 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} when the message size is deterministic. In this case the Laplace transform is not invertible (we only invert it numerically) but the moments have an interesting combinatorial explanation. Fourth, we justify our observation that the “best system” is among 𝒫n,ℬn\mathcal{P}_{n},\mathcal{B}_{n}, for n=1,2n=1,2. We conclude with some words for future work in Section 6.

2 Basic framework

We discuss the technique used in the analysis for all systems described in the introduction from the point of view of the distribution of the age of information. By this phrase, we will always mean that the age of information process α⁡(t)\alpha(t), t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, is stationary and that we shall be interested in the distribution of α⁡(t)\alpha(t) for some, and hence all, tt which will be taken to be the point t=0t=0. The goal is to derive a “fixed point equation” for α⁡(0)\alpha(0), see equation (11) below. We note right away, that the present analysis is different than that of paper [10, 6] as we take advantage of an embedded Markov chain. The arrival process is always taken to be Poisson process on ℝ\mathbb{R} (=time) with rate λ\lambda. As mentioned above, TnT_{n} is the arrival time of message labeled nn. Its size is σn\sigma_{n}. The collection of message sizes are i.i.d. and independent of the arrival process. Let

G⁡(x)=ℙ⁡(σ1≤x)G(x)=\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{1}\leq x)

be the distribution function of the typical size and let 1/μ1/\mu be its expectation, assumed to be finite. Also assume that G⁡(0)=0G(0)=0. Abusing notation, we shall let GG denote the probability measure defined by the function G⁡(x)G(x) and by G^​(s)\hat{G}(s) its Laplace transform:

G^​(s)=∫0∞e−s​x​𝑑G​(x).\hat{G}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sx}dG(x).

Recall that Tn+ΔnT_{n}+\Delta_{n} is defined as the time at which message nn departs either because it was pushed out or rejected or because it was successfully processed (ψn=1\psi_{n}=1 in the latter case). See discussion around (1) and (2) where these symbols were introduced. Then the number of messages in the system at time t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} is given by

ξ⁡(t)=∑n∈ℤ𝟏Tn≤t<Tn+Δn.\xi(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\bm{1}_{T_{n}\leq t<T_{n}+\Delta_{n}}.

Note that if the message is immediately rejected then Δn=0\Delta_{n}=0 and so this message does not contribute to ξ\xi. We let

{Sm,m∈ℤ}:={Tn+Δn:n∈ℤ,ψn=1},\{S_{m},m\in\mathbb{Z}\}:=\{T_{n}+\Delta_{n}:\,n\in\mathbb{Z},\,\psi_{n}=1\},

and, thinking of the two sets as sequences, {Sm}\{S_{m}\} is a subsequence of {Tn+Δn}\{T_{n}+\Delta_{n}\} and is enumerated so that Sm1<Sm2S_{m_{1}}<S_{m_{2}} if m1<m2m_{1}<m_{2}. We note that ξ\xi is right-continuous for all tt. Recalling the notions of Markov renewal and semi-Markov processes, see, e.g., [1, VII.4], our first observation is:

Lemma 1.

For both ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} cases, the process ξ⁡(t)\xi(t), t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, is a semi-Markov process [4, Ch.10] with respect to the points SnS_{n}, n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. Moreover, the distribution of ξ\xi is the same in both ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} cases.

This follows easily by standard arguments in queueing theory, for instance in the analysis of a queue with Poisson arrivals; see, e.g., [4, Ch. 6, Sec. 5]. Thus, ξ\xi does not “see” the difference between ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}. The distinction between these two will become important in the next section when we discuss the details about α\alpha in each case.

We further assume that the arrival process together with the process ξ\xi are stationary under a probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P}. (This assumption is non-vacuous; we shall not elaborate on this further but refer the reader to [2] for an exposition of techniques used to establish it.)

We refer to the intervals [Sn,Sn+1)[S_{n},S_{n+1}) as segments and split the paths of ξ\xi into union of paths over segments. See Figure 2. By convention, we assume that the segment labelled 00 contains the point t=0t=0.

Denote by ℙ0\mathbb{P}^{0} the Palm probability of ℙ\mathbb{P} with respect to the point process {Sn}\{S_{n}\}. We refer to [2] for this concept. Intuitively, ℙ0\mathbb{P}^{0} is ℙ\mathbb{P} conditional on the event that 0∈{Sn,n∈ℤ}0\in\{S_{n},n\in\mathbb{Z}\}. Hence ℙ0​(S0=0)=1\mathbb{P}^{0}(S_{0}=0)=1. Let

Kn:=ξ⁡(Sn),n∈ℤ.K_{n}:=\xi(S_{n}),\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}.

The sequence {Kn}\{K_{n}\} is a Markov chain with state space {0,1}\{0,1\} while {(Sn,Kn)}\{(S_{n},K_{n})\} is the Markov renewal sequence [1, 4] associated to the semi-Markov process ξ\xi. The latter has transition kernel

Qi​j(x):=ℙ0(Sn+1−Sn≤x,Kn+1=j|Kn=i),i,j∈{0,1},Q_{ij}(x):=\mathbb{P}^{0}(S_{n+1}-S_{n}\leq x,K_{n+1}=j\,|\,K_{n}=i),\quad i,j\in\{0,1\},

explicitly given by

[Q00​(x)Q01​(x)Q10​(x)Q11​(x)]=[∫0x(1−e−λ⁡(x−u))​e−λ​u​dG​(u)∫0x(1−e−λ⁡(x−u))​(1−e−λ​u)​dG​(u)∫0xe−λ​u​dG​(u)∫0x(1−e−λ​u)​dG​(u)],\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}Q_{00}(x)&Q_{01}(x)\\ Q_{10}(x)&Q_{11}(x)\end{array}\right]\;=\;\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\int_{0}^{x}\left(1-e^{-\lambda(x-u)}\right)e^{-\lambda u}dG(u)&\int_{0}^{x}\left(1-e^{-\lambda(x-u)}\right)\left(1-e^{-\lambda u}\right)dG(u)\\ &\\ \int_{0}^{x}e^{-\lambda u}dG(u)&\int_{0}^{x}\left(1-e^{-\lambda u}\right)dG(u)\end{array}\right], (6)

as follows easily by considering the cases of Figure 2. Letting x→∞x\rightarrow\infty in (6) we obtain the transition matrix for the Markov chain {Kn}\{K_{n}\},

[Q00​(∞)Q01​(∞)Q10​(∞)Q11​(∞)]=[G^​(λ)1−G^​(λ)G^​(λ)1−G^​(λ)],\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}Q_{00}(\infty)&Q_{01}(\infty)\\ Q_{10}(\infty)&Q_{11}(\infty)\end{array}\right]\;=\;\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\hat{G}(\lambda)&1-\hat{G}(\lambda)\\ \hat{G}(\lambda)&1-\hat{G}(\lambda)\end{array}\right],

from which it is evident that Kn,n≥1K_{n},n\geq 1, is not just Markovian but also a sequence of independent Bernoulli random variables with

ℙ0​(Kn=0)=G^​(λ)=1−ℙ0​(Kn=1).\mathbb{P}^{0}(K_{n}=0)=\hat{G}(\lambda)=1-\mathbb{P}^{0}(K_{n}=1). (7)

Figure 2 shows the four different types of segments depending on the values of KnK_{n} and Kn+1K_{n+1}. We next define

Φi​(s):=𝔼0​[e−s⁡(S1−S0)|K0=i],\Phi_{i}(s):=\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s(S_{1}-S_{0})}|K_{0}=i],

and, using the kernel (6), we obtain

Φ0​(s)\displaystyle\Phi_{0}(s) =∫0∞e−s​x​d​Q00​(x)+∫0∞e−s​x​d​Q01​(x)=λλ+s​G^​(s),\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sx}dQ_{00}(x)+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sx}dQ_{01}(x)=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+s}\,\hat{G}(s), (8)

From (8), (9), and (7) we obtain the Laplace transform of the segment length:

Φ⁡(s):=𝔼0​[e−s⁡(S1−S0)]=(1−G^​(λ)+G^​(λ)​λλ+s)​G^​(s).\Phi(s)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s(S_{1}-S_{0})}]\;=\;\left(1-\hat{G}(\lambda)+\hat{G}(\lambda)\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+s}\right)\,\hat{G}(s).

𝔼0​[S1−S0]=1μ+G^​(λ)λ.\mathbb{E}^{0}[S_{1}-S_{0}]\;=\;\frac{1}{\mu}+\frac{\hat{G}(\lambda)}{\lambda}. (10)

We shall henceforth use the abbreviation 𝔼⁡(X,A)\mathbb{E}(X;A) for the expectation of a random variable XX on the event AA, that is, the quantity 𝔼⁡(X​𝟏A)\mathbb{E}(X\bm{1}_{A}). The following result depends entirely on the semi-Markov property of ξ\xi.

Proposition 1.

The random variable α⁡(0)\alpha(0) satisfies

𝔼⁡[e−s​α​(0)]=λs⋅𝔼0​[e−s​α​(0);K0=0]​(1−λλ+s​G^​(s))+𝔼0​[e−s​α​(0);K0=1]​(1−G^​(s))λμ+G^​(λ).\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha(0)}]\;=\;\frac{\lambda}{s}\cdot\frac{\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(0)};{K_{0}=0}]\,\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+s}\hat{G}(s)\right)+\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(0)};{K_{0}=1}]\,\left(1-\hat{G}(s)\right)}{\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\hat{G}(\lambda)}. (11)
Proof.

The Palm inversion formula [1, 2] applied to the ℙ\mathbb{P}-stationary process α\alpha gives

𝔼⁡[e−s​α​(0)]=𝔼0​[∫S0S1e−s​α​(t)​𝑑t]𝔼0​[S1−S0].\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha(0)}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}^{0}[\int_{S_{0}}^{S_{1}}e^{-s\alpha(t)}dt]}{\mathbb{E}^{0}[S_{1}-S_{0}]}. (12)

Take a look at (3) and notice that the process α\alpha is right-continuous. Its set of discontinuities is {Sn}\{S_{n}\}. Moreover, it increases at unit rate on each segment:

α⁡(t)=α⁡(Sn)+t−Sn, for t∈[Sn,Sn+1).\alpha(t)=\alpha(S_{n})+t-S_{n},\hskip 7.22743pt\mbox{ for $t\in[S_{n},S_{n+1})$.} (13)

To see this, notice that, for Sn≤t<Sn+1S_{n}\leq t<S_{n+1}, we have D⁡(t)=D⁡(Sn)=SnD(t)=D(S_{n})=S_{n}, by the definition of DD in (1), and so A⁡(D⁡(t))=A⁡(D⁡(Sn))=A⁡(Sn)A(D(t))=A(D(S_{n}))=A(S_{n}). Since, from the definition (3), α⁡(t)=t−A⁡(D⁡(t))\alpha(t)=t-A(D(t)) for all tt, we have

α⁡(t)=t−A⁡(Sn),\alpha(t)=t-A(S_{n}),

whenever Sn≤t<Sn+1S_{n}\leq t<S_{n+1}. Writing this for t=Snt=S_{n}, we have

α⁡(Sn)=Sn−A⁡(Sn),\alpha(S_{n})=S_{n}-A(S_{n}),

and so (13) is obtained by subtracting the last two displays. In particular, S0=0S_{0}=0 and α⁡(t)=α⁡(0)+t\alpha(t)=\alpha(0)+t for t∈[S0,S1)t\in[S_{0},S_{1}), ℙ0\mathbb{P}^{0}-a.s. Hence, for i=0,1i=0,1,

𝔼0​[∫S0S1e−s​α​(t)​𝑑t;K0=i]=𝔼0​[e−s​α​(0)​1−e−s​S1s;K0=i]=s−1​Φi​(s)​𝔼0​[e−s​α​(0);K0=i],\mathbb{E}^{0}\left[\int_{S_{0}}^{S_{1}}e^{-s\alpha(t)}dt;{K_{0}=i}\right]=\mathbb{E}^{0}\left[e^{-s\alpha(0)}\,\frac{1-e^{-sS_{1}}}{s};{K_{0}=i}\right]=s^{-1}\Phi_{i}(s)\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(0)};{K_{0}=i}], (14)

where the last equality follows from the fact that α⁡(0)\alpha(0) and S1−S0S_{1}-S_{0} are conditionally independent given {K0=i}\{K_{0}=i\}, a consequence of the semi-Markov structure of the process {ξ⁡(t)}\{\xi(t)\}, see Lemma 1. Using expressions (8) and (9) and adding the terms in (14) we obtain the numerator of (12). The denominator is given by (10). This shows the validity of (11). ∎

Remark 1.

It should be clear that (11) holds for a much larger class of systems with one (or several independent) Poisson arrival process(es). For example, we may define ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} to be an extension of ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} when the buffer has nn cells where messages are stored according to the order of their arrivals and a message arriving to a full buffer is immediately rejected (the so-called M/GI/1/nn queue). On the other hand, we may define 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} to be an extension of 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}: messages are stored in an order that is reverse to their order of arrival; so if there is a message being processed in cell 1 at time tt, the message in cell 2 arrived last before tt while the message in cell nn is the oldest; a new message arriving at a full buffer is always stored in cell 2, displacing the other messages upwards and expels the one sitting in cell 1 (oldest one). In both ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} and 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}, the process ξ\xi is semi-Markov and thus Proposition 1, depending only on this semi-Markov property, applies and formula (11) holds. In fact, one can assert that proposition holds for networks with i.i.d. message sojourn times, e.g., due to a single bottleneck server.. We shall not attempt to formalize this further in this paper.

3 The ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} system

Recall that the ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} system is the same as a single server queue with buffer size 2. Under our Poisson assumption for the arrival process and i.i.d. assumptions for message sizes, this is further denoted by M/GI/1/2 in standard queueing theory. We are, however, interested not in the number of messages in the system neither on message delays but, rather, on the age of information process α\alpha. Assuming that α\alpha is stationary, we compute the Laplace transform of α⁡(0)\alpha(0) under ℙ\mathbb{P} by using (11) which requires knowledge of 𝔼0​[e−s​α​(0);K0=j]\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(0)};{K_{0}=j}], j=0,1j=0,1. To obtain the latter, we consider the segment [S−1,S0)[S_{-1},S_{0}) and further condition on K−1K_{-1} and summarize the results in Lemma 2 below. In what follows, we let τ,σ\tau,\sigma be two independent random variables, where τ\tau is exponential with rate λ\lambda and σ\sigma has distribution GG.

Lemma 2.

For ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2},

𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=0,K0=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=0}] =G^​(λ)​G^​(s+λ),\displaystyle=\hat{G}(\lambda)\hat{G}(s+\lambda), (15)
𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=0,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1}] =G^​(λ)​(G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ)),\displaystyle=\hat{G}(\lambda)\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right), (16)
𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=1,K0=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=0}] =λλ−s​(G^​(s)−G^​(λ))​G^​(s+λ),\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}\,\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(\lambda)\right)\hat{G}(s+\lambda), (17)
𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=1,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=1}] =λλ−s​(G^​(s)−G^​(λ))​(G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ)).\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}\,\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(\lambda)\right)\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right). (18)
Proof.

Recall that the KnK_{n} are i.i.d. with distribution (7): ℙ0​(Kn=0)=G^​(λ)\mathbb{P}^{0}(K_{n}=0)=\hat{G}(\lambda). We shall consider the four cases separately and, in each case, we shall be referring to the definition (3) to figure out what α⁡(0)\alpha(0) is.

Case 1. K−1=0,K0=0K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=0. Observe α⁡(0)=S0−T0\alpha(0)=S_{0}-T_{0}, see Figure 3. But

ℙ0​(S0−T0∈d​x∣K0=0,K−1=0)=ℙ⁡(σ∈d​x∣σ<τ)=e−λ​x​d​G​(x)G^​(λ),\mathbb{P}^{0}(S_{0}-T_{0}\in dx\mid K_{0}=0,K_{-1}=0)\;=\;\mathbb{P}(\sigma\in dx\mid\sigma<\tau)\;=\;\frac{e^{-\lambda x}dG(x)}{\hat{G}(\lambda)},

and so

𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=0,K0=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=0}] =\displaystyle= ∫0∞e−s​x​e−λ​xG^​(λ)​𝑑G​(x)​(G^​(λ))2=G^​(λ)​G^​(s+λ).\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sx}\frac{e^{-\lambda x}}{\hat{G}(\lambda)}dG(x)\left(\hat{G}(\lambda)\right)^{2}\;=\;\hat{G}(\lambda)\hat{G}(s+\lambda).

Case 2. K−1=0,K0=1K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1. We have α⁡(0)=S0−T−1\alpha(0)=S_{0}-T_{-1}, see Figure 3. Since

ℙ0​(S0−T−1∈d​x∣K0=1,K−1=0)=ℙ⁡(σ∈d​x∣τ<σ)=(1−e−λ​x)​d​G​(x)1−G^​(λ)\mathbb{P}^{0}(S_{0}-T_{-1}\in dx\mid K_{0}=1,K_{-1}=0)\;=\;\mathbb{P}(\sigma\in dx\mid\tau<\sigma)\;=\;\frac{\left(1-e^{-\lambda x}\right)dG(x)}{1-\hat{G}(\lambda)}

we obtain

𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=0,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1}] =\displaystyle= ℙ0(K−1=0,K0=1)𝔼0[e−s​α​(S0)∣K−1=0,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{0}(K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1)\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})}\mid K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1]
=G^​(λ)​∫0∞e−s​x​(1−e−λ​x)​𝑑G​(x)=G^​(λ)​(G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ)).\displaystyle\hskip-101.17755pt=\;\hat{G}(\lambda)\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sx}\left(1-e^{-\lambda x}\right)dG(x)\;=\;\hat{G}(\lambda)\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right).

Case 3. K−1=1,K0=0K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=0. To figure out α⁡(0)\alpha(0) we are here forced to consider two consecutive segments. We then have

α⁡(0)=(S0−S−1)+(S−1−T0),\alpha(0)=\left(S_{0}-S_{-1}\right)+\left(S_{-1}-T_{0}\right),

see Figure 4. Note that

S0−S−1S_{0}-S_{-1} and S−1−T0S_{-1}-T_{0} are conditionally independent given K−1=1K_{-1}=1

with ℙ0(S0−S−1∈dx;K0=0∣K−1=1)=ℙ(σ∈dx;σ<τ)\mathbb{P}^{0}(S_{0}-S_{-1}\in dx;K_{0}=0\mid K_{-1}=1)=\mathbb{P}(\sigma\in dx;\sigma<\tau) and ℙ0(S−1−T0∈dx;K−1=1∣K−2=0)=ℙ(σ−τ∈dx;σ>τ)\mathbb{P}^{0}(S_{-1}-T_{0}\in dx;K_{-1}=1\mid K_{-2}=0)=\mathbb{P}(\sigma-\tau\in dx;\sigma>\tau), respectively. Thus

𝔼0​[e−s​α​(0);K−1=1,K0=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(0)};{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=0}] =\displaystyle= 𝔼⁡[e−s​σ;σ<τ]​𝔼​[e−s⁡(σ−τ);σ>τ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\sigma};{\sigma<\tau}]\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-s(\sigma-\tau)};{\sigma>\tau}]
=𝔼⁡[e−s​σ​e−λ​σ]​𝔼​[e−s​σ​∫0σλ​e−(λ−s)​t​𝑑t]=G^​(s+λ)​λλ−s​(G^​(s)−G^​(λ)).\displaystyle\hskip-72.26999pt\;=\;\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\sigma}e^{-\lambda\sigma}]\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\sigma}\int_{0}^{\sigma}\lambda e^{-(\lambda-s)t}dt]\;=\;\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(\lambda)\right).

Case 4. Again, we have to consider two consecutive segments to realize that

α⁡(0)=S0−T−1=(S−1−T−1)+(S0−S−1),\alpha(0)=S_{0}-T_{-1}=\left(S_{-1}-T_{-1}\right)+\left(S_{0}-S_{-1}\right),

see Figure 5. The two random variables

(S−1−T−1)\left(S_{-1}-T_{-1}\right) and (S0−S−1)\left(S_{0}-S_{-1}\right) are conditionally independent given that K−1=1K_{-1}=1

and thus

𝔼0​[e−s​α​(0);K−1=1,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(0)};{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=1}] =\displaystyle= 𝔼0​[e−s⁡(S−1−T−1)−s⁡(S0−S−1);K−1=1,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\left(S_{-1}-T_{-1}\right)-s\left(S_{0}-S_{-1}\right)};{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=1}]
=𝔼⁡[e−s⁡(σ−τ);σ>τ]​𝔼​[e−s​σ;σ>τ]=𝔼⁡[∫0σe−s⁡(σ−t)​λ​e−λ​t​𝑑t]​𝔼​[e−s​σ​(1−e−λ​σ)]\displaystyle\hskip-101.17755pt=\;\mathbb{E}[e^{-s(\sigma-\tau)};{\sigma>\tau}]\,\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\sigma};{\sigma>\tau}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{\sigma}e^{-s(\sigma-t)}\lambda e^{-\lambda t}dt\right]\,\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-s\sigma}\left(1-e^{-\lambda\sigma}\right)\right]
=λλ−s​(G^​(s)−G^​(λ))​(G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ)).\displaystyle\hskip-101.17755pt=\;\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(\lambda)\right)\,\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right).

This completes the proof. ∎

Define

G^I​(s)=1−G^​(s)s​μ.\hat{G}_{I}(s)=\frac{1-\hat{G}(s)}{s}\mu. (19)

This is the Laplace transform of a probability measure GIG_{I} that is well-known in renewal theory: If we consider a renewal process with points, say, ZnZ_{n}, n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, such that Z0=0Z_{0}=0 and Zn+1−ZnZ_{n+1}-Z_{n} having distribution GG, then there it has a stationary version (with no point at 00) and in such a way that Z1Z_{1} has distribution GIG_{I}.

Theorem 1.

For ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}, the Laplace transform of the stationary Age of Information is given by

𝔼⁡[e−s​α​(0)]=G^​(s)​(G^​(λ)+λ​G^​(s)−G^​(λ)λ−s)​(G^​(λ)λμ+G^​(λ)​λλ+s​G^​(s+λ)G^​(λ)+λμλμ+G^​(λ)​G^I​(s)).\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha(0)}]\;=\;\hat{G}(s)\,\left(\hat{G}(\lambda)+\lambda\frac{\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(\lambda)}{\lambda-s}\right)\,\left(\frac{\hat{G}(\lambda)}{\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\hat{G}(\lambda)}\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+s}\frac{\hat{G}(s+\lambda)}{\hat{G}(\lambda)}+\frac{\frac{\lambda}{\mu}}{\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\hat{G}(\lambda)}\hat{G}_{I}(s)\right). (20)
Proof.

Summing (15) and (16) we obtain

𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K0=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{0}=0}] =\displaystyle= G^​(s+λ)​[λλ−s​G^​(s)−sλ−s​G^​(λ)]\displaystyle\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\left[\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}\hat{G}(s)-\frac{s}{\lambda-s}\hat{G}(\lambda)\right]
𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{0}=1}] =\displaystyle= (G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ))​[λλ−s​G^​(s)−sλ−s​G^​(λ)].\displaystyle\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right)\left[\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}\hat{G}(s)-\frac{s}{\lambda-s}\hat{G}(\lambda)\right].

Substituting the last two lines into the right hand side of (11) we obtain

𝔼⁡[e−s​α​(0)]=G^​(s)​[λλ−s​G^​(s)−sλ−s​G^​(λ)]​(G^​(s+λ)s+λ+1−G^​(s)s)1λ​(λμ+G^​(λ)),\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha(0)}]=\frac{\hat{G}(s)\left[\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-s}\hat{G}(s)-\frac{s}{\lambda-s}\hat{G}(\lambda)\right]\left(\frac{\hat{G}(s+\lambda)}{s+\lambda}+\frac{1-\hat{G}(s)}{s}\right)}{\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\hat{G}(\lambda)\right)}, (21)

which gives (20) if we take into account the definition of G^I\hat{G}_{I}. ∎

Corollary 1.

Expression (20) gives the stationary AoI as a sum of three independent random variables. In particular, the middle term in the right hand side of (20) corresponds to the Laplace transform of the random variable (σ−τ)+(\sigma-\tau)^{+}. Moreover, the expectation of α⁡(0)\alpha(0) is given by

𝔼⁡[α⁡(0)]=2μ−1−G^​(λ)λ+G^​(λ)−λ​G^′​(λ)+12​λ2​∫0∞x2​𝑑G​(x)λ​(λμ+G^​(λ)).\mathbb{E}[\alpha(0)]\;=\;\frac{2}{\mu}-\frac{1-\hat{G}(\lambda)}{\lambda}+\frac{\hat{G}(\lambda)-\lambda\hat{G}^{\prime}(\lambda)+\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{2}dG(x)}{\lambda\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}+\hat{G}(\lambda)\right)}.

We obtained this corollary directly from the Laplace transform (20) where we recognize that 12​μ​∫0∞x2​𝑑G​(x)=∫0∞x​d​BI​(x)\frac{1}{2}\mu\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{2}dG(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}xdB_{I}(x). Notice that if the message size has high variance then so does 𝔼​α​(0)\mathbb{E}\alpha(0). In particular, 𝔼​α​(0)=∞\mathbb{E}\alpha(0)=\infty if ∫x2​𝑑G​(x)=∞\int x^{2}dG(x)=\infty. Rather than seeing this as a problem, one should change the point of view and adopt another function of α\alpha as a performance measure, for instance, 𝔼​α​(0)p\mathbb{E}\alpha(0)^{p} for some p<1p<1.

Corollary 2.

For ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}, with GG being exponential with mean 1/μ1/\mu we have

𝔼⁡[e−s​α​(0)]=(μs+μ)3​λs+λ​s2+2​s​(λ+μ)+λ2+λ​μ+μ2(λ2+λ​μ+μ2),\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha(0)}]\;=\;\left(\frac{\mu}{s+\mu}\right)^{3}\frac{\lambda}{s+\lambda}\,\frac{s^{2}+2s(\lambda+\mu)+\lambda^{2}+\lambda\mu+\mu^{2}}{\left(\lambda^{2}+\lambda\mu+\mu^{2}\right)}, (22)
𝔼⁡[α⁡(0)]=3​λ3+2​λ2​μ+2​λ​μ2+μ3λ​μ​(λ2+λ​μ+μ2).\mathbb{E}[\alpha(0)]\;=\;\frac{3\lambda^{3}+2\lambda^{2}\mu+2\lambda\mu^{2}+\mu^{3}}{\lambda\mu\left(\lambda^{2}+\lambda\mu+\mu^{2}\right)}. (23)

Inverting the last Laplace transform gives a measure with density equal to (4). Interestingly, as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty we immediately see from (22) that 𝔼⁡[e−s​α​(0)]→(μ/(s+μ))3\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha(0)}]\to(\mu/(s+\mu))^{3}, the Laplace transform of the sum of 3 i.i.d. exponentials. See Section 5.4 for an explanation of this.

4 The 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} system

We remind the reader that 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} differs from ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} in that the arriving message is always admitted by replacing the message (if any) sitting in the second cell of the buffer, see Figure 1. Again, 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} is not service-preemptive: once a message starts being processed it will not be interrupted. The strategy for obtaining the Laplace transform of α⁡(0)\alpha(0) is the same as before. We make use of (11) of Proposition 1 which needs computation of the quantities involving α⁡(0)\alpha(0) in its right-hand side. The analog of Lemma 2 is Lemma 3 below which looks conspicuously the same. In fact, the first two formulas are identical. The last two differ.

Lemma 3.

For 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2},

𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=0,K0=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=0}] =G^​(λ)​G^​(s+λ),\displaystyle=\hat{G}(\lambda)\hat{G}(s+\lambda), (24)
𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=0,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1}] =G^​(λ)​(G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ)),\displaystyle=\hat{G}(\lambda)\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right), (25)
𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=1,K0=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=0}] =λλ+s​(1−G^​(s+λ))​G^​(s+λ),\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+s}\left(1-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right)\,\hat{G}(s+\lambda), (26)
𝔼0​[e−s​α​(S0);K−1=1,K0=1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s\alpha(S_{0})};{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=1}] =λλ+s​(1−G^​(λ+s))​(G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ))\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+s}\left(1-\hat{G}(\lambda+s)\right)\,\left(\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)\right) (27)
Proof.

1) When K−1=0,K0=0K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=0 or when K−1=0,K0=1K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1 the AoI same as in the ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} system, the reason being that the number of messages in the system is always at most 1, see Figure 3.

2) Suppose next that K−1=1,K0=0K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=0. In Figure 6 we depict the two scenaria corresponding to the possible values of K−2K_{-2}, namely (K−2,K−1,K0)=(0,1,0)(K_{-2},K_{-1},K_{0})=(0,1,0) or (1,1,0)(1,1,0). In both cases, (3) and the system dynamics imply that

α⁡(0)=S0−S−1+V,\alpha(0)=S_{0}-S_{-1}+V,

VV is the time elapsed between the last arrival in the interval (S−2,S−1)(S_{-2},S_{-1}) and S−1S_{-1}. If there is only one arrival in this interval then V:=S−1−T0V:=S_{-1}-T_{0}. In any case,

conditionally on {K−1=1,K0=0}\{K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=0\}, the random variables VV and S0−S−1S_{0}-S_{-1} are independent.

Therefore,

𝔼0[e−s⁡(S0−S−1+V)∣K−1=0,K0=1]=𝔼0[e−s⁡(S0−S−1)∣K−1=0,K0=1]𝔼0[e−s​V∣K−1=0,K0=1]\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s(S_{0}-S_{-1}+V)}\mid K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1]=\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s(S_{0}-S_{-1})}\mid K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1]\,\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-sV}\mid K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1]

and the first factor on the right is easy:

𝔼0[e−s⁡(S0−S−1)∣K−1=0,K0=1]=∫0∞e−s​xe−λ​x​d​G​(x)G^​(λ)=G^​(s+λ)G^​(λ).\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s(S_{0}-S_{-1})}\mid K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1]\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sx}\frac{e^{-\lambda x}dG(x)}{\hat{G}(\lambda)}\;=\;\frac{\hat{G}(s+\lambda)}{\hat{G}(\lambda)}.

To evaluate 𝔼0[e−s​V∣K−1=0,K0=1]\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-sV}\mid K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1] we note that, VV is the distance of the last Poisson point inside the interval (T−1,S−1)(T_{-1},S_{-1}) (in the left scenario of Figure 6) or the interval (T−1,S−1)(T_{-1},S_{-1}) in the right scenario. (In both cases the length of the interval is that of a message size conditioned on containing at least one Poisson point.) To obtain the Laplace transform of VV look backward in time starting from S−1S_{-1} until the first Poisson point appears and condition on the event that this occurs between S−1S_{-1} and S−2S_{-2}. Thus, the density of VV at v>0v>0 is

(1−G⁡(v))​λ​e−λ​v1−G^​(λ),\frac{(1-G(v))\lambda e^{-\lambda v}}{1-\hat{G}(\lambda)},

which gives

𝔼0[e−s​V∣K−1=0,K0=1]=∫0∞e−s​vλ​e−λ​v​(1−G⁡(v))1−G^​(λ)dv=λλ+s1−G^​(s+λ)1−G^​(λ).\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-sV}\mid K_{-1}=0,K_{0}=1]\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sv}\frac{\lambda e^{-\lambda v}(1-G(v))}{1-\hat{G}(\lambda)}dv\;=\;\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+s}\,\frac{1-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)}{1-\hat{G}(\lambda)}. (28)

Putting these together we obtain (26).

3) Finally, assume that K−1=1,K0=1K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=1. This situation is similar to the previous one and thus will be treated succinctly. We are guided by Figure 7. Firstly, we have

𝔼0[e−s⁡(S0−S−1)∣K−1=1,K0=1]=∫0∞e−s​x1−e−λ​x​d​G​(x)1−G^​(λ)=G^​(s)−G^​(s+λ)1−G^​(λ).\mathbb{E}^{0}[e^{-s(S_{0}-S_{-1})}\mid K_{-1}=1,K_{0}=1]\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-sx}\frac{1-e^{-\lambda x}dG(x)}{1-\hat{G}(\lambda)}\;=\;\frac{\hat{G}(s)-\hat{G}(s+\lambda)}{1-\hat{G}(\lambda)}.

The formula for 𝔼​e−s​α​(0)\mathbb{E}e^{-s\alpha(0)} now clear.

Theorem 2.

For 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, the Laplace transform of the stationary Age of Information is given by

5 Comparisons and optimality

Slightly abusing notation, we write α𝒫n\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}} instead of α𝒫n​(0)\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}}(0); To further simplify life, we shall now use normalized units, assuming μ=1\mu=1. We draw conclusions from the work above, as well as the results of [14, 6, 10], attempting to justify our claim that “small buffers suffice”. We first summarize observations regarding 𝒫n,ℬn\mathcal{P}_{n},\mathcal{B}_{n}, n=1,2n=1,2, and then consider larger nn.

5.1 Recalling formulas for 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} and ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}

Concerning the 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} system we have, from [10, Corollary 4],

𝔼⁡[e−s​α𝒫1]=ρ​G^​(s+ρ)s+ρ​G^​(s+ρ),𝔼⁡[α𝒫1]=1ρ​G^​(ρ).\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}}]=\frac{\rho\hat{G}(s+\rho)}{s+\rho\hat{G}(s+\rho)},\quad\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}]=\frac{1}{\rho\hat{G}(\rho)}. (34)

On the other hand, for ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}, [10, Corollary 9(i)], gives

𝔼⁡[e−s​αℬ1]=ρ1+ρ⋅(s+ρ−ρ​G^​(s))​G^​(s)s⁡(s+ρ),𝔼⁡[αℬ1]=1+1ρ+ρ2⋅𝔼​σ21+ρ.\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}}]=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}\cdot\frac{(s+\rho-\rho\hat{G}(s))\hat{G}(s)}{s(s+\rho)},\quad\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}]=1+\frac{1}{\rho}+\frac{\rho}{2}\cdot\frac{\mathbb{E}\sigma^{2}}{1+\rho}. (35)

We now have information about all systems that we now compare. The comparisons depend on the message size distributions. We choose to consider two “extremes”. First, exponentially distributed size, second, deterministic, representing maximal and minimal randomness. The observations are summarized in plots rather than formulas because the latter, albeit explicit in almost all cases (but see §5.5 below for an exception), are not succinctly presentable.

5.2 Exponential message sizes

We obtain explicit formulas from Corollary 2 for αℬ2\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}, Corollary 4 for α𝒫2\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{2}} and (35), (34), for αℬ1\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}, α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}, respectively. Using the notation M𝒫1​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}(\rho) for 𝔼⁡[α𝒫1]\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}], where ρ=λ/μ=λ\rho=\lambda/\mu=\lambda, in normalized units. Similarly for other systems. We summarize the comparisons in a plot:

We see that

M𝒫1​(ρ)<M𝒫2​(ρ)<Mℬ2​(ρ)​ for all ρ. M_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}(\rho)<M_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(\rho)<M_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}(\rho)\text{ for all $\rho$. }

The odd system is ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}. For small ρ\rho, Mℬ1​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}(\rho) is worst (highest). For large ρ\rho, Mℬ1​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}(\rho) is between M𝒫1​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}(\rho) and M𝒫2​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(\rho). There is also an intermediate zone, where Mℬ1​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}(\rho) is between M𝒫2​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(\rho) and Mℬ2​(ρ)M_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}(\rho).

We can also ask whether the comparisons above remain true in the sense of stochastic ordering. Recall that a real random variable XX is stochastically smaller than YY, and write

X<stYX<_{\text{st}}Y, if ℙ⁡(X>u)≤ℙ⁡(Y>u)\mathbb{P}(X>u)\leq\mathbb{P}(Y>u) for all u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}.

Note that stochastic ordering is a partial order in the space of probability measures on the real line so two random variables may not be comparable at all. The information is obtained by inverting the Laplace transforms (22) and (32) which give the densities (4) and (5), respectively. It is also easy to invert the Laplace transforms (34) and (35). α𝒫1<stα𝒫2<stαℬ2 for all ρ.\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}\text{ for all }\rho.

α𝒫1<stαℬ1<stα𝒫2 for all sufficiently high ρ.\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}\text{ for all sufficiently high }\rho.

5.3 Deterministic message sizes

We now assume that ℙ⁡(σ=1)=1\mathbb{P}(\sigma=1)=1: message sizes are all equal to 11 with probability 11. We can thus easily obtain M⁡(ρ)M(\rho) in all cases by setting σ=1\sigma=1 in the formulas of Corollaries 1 and 3 and in (35) and (34). They are summarized in Figure 11. We observe that

M𝒫2​(ρ)<Mℬ2​(ρ)<M𝒫1​(ρ)​ for all ρ. M_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(\rho)<M_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}(\rho)<M_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}(\rho)\text{ for all $\rho$. }

limρ→∞M𝒫1​(ρ)=∞.\lim_{\rho\to\infty}M_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}(\rho)=\infty.

The worst system, from the point of view of expectation, is thus 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1}. To obtain information about ℙ⁡(α𝒫1>x)\mathbb{P}(\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}>x) for all xx, we resort to numerics as the Laplace transform (34) with G^​(s)=e−s\hat{G}(s)=e^{-s} is not invertible. α𝒫2<stαℬ2<stα𝒫1,αℬ1<stα𝒫1 for all ρ,\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}},\,\,\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}\text{ for all }\rho,

whereas αℬ1\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}} is not comparable to any of the other three random variables. Figure 13 shows the densities for α𝒫2\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{2}} and αℬ2\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{2}} for various values of ρ\rho.

5.4 High traffic asymptotics

“High traffic asymptotics” refers to the regime ρ→∞\rho\to\infty. Even though we have no explicit formulas for 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} or ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} when n≥3n\geq 3, we can easily obtain asymptotics from the system dynamics.

Proposition 2.

Let σ,σ1,σ2,…\sigma,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots be i.i.d. copies of σ\sigma. Let σI\sigma_{I} be distributed as G^I\hat{G}_{I} as in (19). Then

α𝒫n→ρ→∞dσ+σI,n≥2,\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}}\xrightarrow[\rho\to\infty]{\text{\rm d}}\sigma+\sigma_{I},\quad n\geq 2,

while

αℬn→ρ→∞dσ1+⋯+σn+σI,n≥1.\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}\xrightarrow[\rho\to\infty]{\text{\rm d}}\sigma_{1}+\cdots+\sigma_{n}+\sigma_{I},\quad n\geq 1.
Sketch of proof.

In both systems, the buffer consists of nn cells. The message being processed sits in cell 11. In 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n}, the freshest message is either in cell 1, in which case all other cells are empty, or in cell 2. When ρ\rho is high there is always a message being processed in cell 1 and the freshest message is in cell 2. Hence, at any time tt, the AoI α𝒫n​(t)\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}}(t) equals the service time of the message in cell 2 plus the remaining service time of the message in cell 1. These are two independent random variables. The first one is distributed as σ\sigma. The second is distributed as σI\sigma_{I} since the system is stationary. For ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}, we can obtain the limit from the Laplace transform of (35). It is easy to to see that limρ→∞𝔼⁡[e−s​αℬ1]=G^​(s)​G^I​(s)\lim_{\rho\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}}]=\hat{G}(s)\,\hat{G}_{I}(s) and so αℬ1→ρ→∞dσ+σI\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{1}}\xrightarrow[\rho\to\infty]{\text{\rm d}}\sigma+\sigma_{I}. For general nn, when ρ\rho is high, the AoI αℬn​(t)\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(t) equals the remaining service time of the message in cell 1 (in distribution equal to σI\sigma_{I}) plus the time elapsed until the beginning of its service which is, in distribution, equal to the sum of nn independent service times. ∎

Remark 2.

When σ=1\sigma=1 with probability 11, σI\sigma_{I} is a uniform random variable in the interval [0,1][0,1]. Hence σ1+⋯+σn+σI=n+σI\sigma_{1}+\cdots+\sigma_{n}+\sigma_{I}=n+\sigma_{I} and the variance of this random variable is 1/121/12, in agreement with the observation around Figure 14 for ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} and ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}. Similarly, for 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, the asymptotic variance is again 1/121/12. In fact, the limits in Proposition 2 also explain the asymptotic shapes of the densities in Figure 13.
The limits of the variances in Figure 14 for ℬ1,ℬ2,𝒫2\mathcal{B}_{1},\mathcal{B}_{2},\mathcal{P}_{2} are also explainable in the light of the proposition above.

It remains to see what the limit of α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} is as ρ→∞\rho\to\infty. This should be considered separately as the limit very much depends on the distribution of σ\sigma. If σ=1\sigma=1 with probability 1, we explained above why α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} converges to a random variable that takes value ∞\infty with probability 1. In fact, this should be true if σ\sigma has a distribution whose support is at positive distance from 00. If σ\sigma is exponential with mean 1, we see directly from (34), that limρ→∞𝔼⁡[e−s​α𝒫1]=1/(s+1)\lim_{\rho\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}}]=1/(s+1). Thus the limit of α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} depends both on the tail of the distribution and on its behavior at 00.

5.5 On the distribution of α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} for deterministic message size

We now complete the discussion in §5.3 by giving some more information on α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}, when σ=1\sigma=1 with probability 1, whose distribution is not explicitly computable but has some interesting properties, including a combinatorial explanation of all of its moments. Another reason we devote a little more ink on α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} is that it seems to be an upper bound on the age of information so long as message sizes are close to being deterministic. From (34) with G^​(s)=exp⁡(−s)\hat{G}(s)=\exp(-s), we have

𝔼⁡[e−s​α𝒫​1]=1m​s​es+1=:Lm​(s),\mathbb{E}[e^{-s\alpha_{\mathcal{P}1}}]=\frac{1}{m\,se^{s}+1}=:L_{m}(s),

with

m:=eρ/ρ=𝔼⁡[α𝒫1].m:=e^{\rho}/\rho=\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}].

This Laplace transform cannot be analytically inverted. However, since Lm​(s)L_{m}(s) as a function of a complex variable ss has no singularity on the closed right-half plane Re⁡(s)≥0\operatorname{Re}(s)\geq 0, we used the inversion formula [13, §8.2]

fm​(t)=12​π​∫−∞∞ei​y1+i​m​y​ei​y​𝑑y,f_{m}(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{iy}}{1+imye^{iy}}dy,

together with a numerical approximation of this extended Riemann integral in order to obtain information about the tail of the distribution of α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} which is plotted in Figure 12 as a dotted line. We can make a few remarks about fmf_{m}.

First, it is obviously a probability density function for all m≥em\geq e since we know that infρ>0eρ/ρ=e\inf_{\rho>0}e^{\rho}/\rho=e. One might conjecture that fmf_{m} remains a probability density function for all m≥0m\geq 0. However, LmL_{m} seizes to be completely monotone [5, XIII.4] for mm small enough and thus, the conjecture is false. To see this, it is easy to see that

Lm′′(s)<0 for s in a neighborhood of zero if (and only if) m<1.L^{\prime\prime}_{m}(s)<0\text{ for $s$ in a neighborhood of zero if (and only if) }m<1.

We strengthen the conjecture by claiming that

Conjecture 1.

Let m≥0m\geq 0. Then Lm​(s)=1/(m​s​es+1)L_{m}(s)=1/(mse^{s}+1) is the Laplace transform of some random variable if and only if m=0m=0 (corresponding to a trivial random variable) or m≥em\geq e.

Second, since Lm​(s)L_{m}(s) is infinitely differentiable at all s≥0s\geq 0, we have that all moments of α𝒫1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} exist. Using a formal series expansion, we can easily express the pp-th moment in terms of the polynomial

Qp(z):=∑k=1p(p)kkp−kzk,p=1,2,…Q_{p}(z):=\sum_{k=1}^{p}(p)_{k}k^{p-k}z^{k},\quad p=1,2,\ldots

as follows

𝔼⁡[α𝒫1p]=(−1)p​Qp​(−m),\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}^{p}]=(-1)^{p}Q_{p}(-m),

with m=eρ/ρm=e^{\rho}/\rho, and then show that this is correct. It is easy to see that Qp​(z)Q_{p}(z) has a combinatorial interpretation. It is the generating function of the sequence (p)k​kp−k(p)_{k}\,k^{p-k}, 1≤k≤p1\leq k\leq p, where (p)k=p(p−1)⋯(p−k+1)(p)_{k}=p(p-1)\cdots(p-k+1), counting the number of ways to form kk labeled groups, each with a distinct leader, using pp different people. For values and other properties, see [15]. One can also see that, for pp large,

𝔼⁡[α𝒫1p]≈p!​mp,\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}^{p}]\approx p!m^{p},

that is, the pp-th moment of an exponential random variable with the same mean.

5.6 The best systems

We now return to the problem of choosing the best system so that we keep AoI “as small as possible”. Even though we have no proof for the optimal system, we have enough reasons to justify making the following conjecture.

Conjecture 2.

Consider the collection 𝒫n,ℬn\mathcal{P}_{n},\mathcal{B}_{n}, n=1,2,…n=1,2,\ldots Assume that each system is driven by a Poisson arrival process of rate λ\lambda. Then, regardless of the message size distribution,

αℐ<stα𝒥\alpha_{\mathcal{I}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{J}}

for all ℐ∈{𝒫1,ℬ1,𝒫2,ℬ2}\mathcal{I}\in\{\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{B}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2},\mathcal{B}_{2}\} and all 𝒥∈{𝒫n,ℬn,n≥3}\mathcal{J}\in\{\mathcal{P}_{n},\mathcal{B}_{n},\,n\geq 3\}.

Evidence for this conjecture is provided by the results of [6, 10], the results in this paper and the following observations. First, it is clear that

α𝒫n​(t)≤αℬn​(t), for all ​t​ and all ​n≥2\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}}(t)\leq\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{n}}(t),\text{ for all }t\text{ and all }n\geq 2

provided that all systems are driven by identical arrival processes and the same sequence of message sizes. In other words, this is a pathwise inequality. Similarly,

αℬ2​(t)≤αℬ3​(t)≤⋯≤αℬ∞​(t), for all ​t.\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{2}}(t)\leq\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{3}}(t)\leq\cdots\leq\alpha_{\mathcal{B}_{\infty}}(t),\text{ for all }t.

One can show that we cannot expect a similar pathwise inequality for the 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} systems. But when ρ\rho is sufficiently large, we showed that, for all n≥2n\geq 2, α𝒫n​(t)\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}}(t) is approximately distributed as σ+σI\sigma+\sigma_{I}, so there is no reason to believe that α𝒫n+1\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n+1}} will improve α𝒫n\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{n}} at high ρ\rho. A crucial step in proving the veracity of the last conjecture would be to show that, in stationarity,

α𝒫2<stα𝒫3<st⋯\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}<_{\text{st}}\alpha_{\mathcal{P}_{3}}<_{\text{st}}\cdots

Thus if the conjecture is true then it would be irrelevant to consider any system other than 𝒫1,𝒫2,ℬ1,ℬ2\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2},\mathcal{B}_{1},\mathcal{B}_{2} insofar as stochastically minimizing the stationary AoI is concerned. However, see [12].

6 Some final words

Using the Markov embedding and Palm inversion formula, we derived the stationary AoI distribution of ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} under Poisson message arrivals and generally distributed message sizes (processing times). The AoI of these systems and two other systems with low AoI, ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} and 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1}, were compared for exponential and deterministic service times, which, in some sense, are two extremes. We paid particular importance to their complementary distribution functions which play a role in important performance requirements. 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} has generally lower AoI for exponentially distributed message sizes, while 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} had lower AoI for deterministic message sizes when the traffic load was sufficiently low. The performance of ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} is interesting, having smallest AoI among these four considered policies in some cases. The ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} system may need to be used instead of these other three owing to technological constraints.

The rules of thumb derived can roughly be summarized as follows: If the message sizes are deterministic or nearly so then it is best to use ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} or 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}, which is pretty close to ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}. In particular, 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} seems to be an upper bound for AoI and this is the reason that we paid some special attention to it in §5.5 (where we had to resort to analytical tricks to approximate it, as there is no closed-form formula for the distribution). On the other hand, if message sizes are “very random”, we expect the opposite: 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} performs best stochastically so. Granted, the study in this paper has been done only for Poisson arrivals and so, to be able to analyze general renewal arrivals and service times one should use a different method which we leave for future work. We should also mention that dynamic policies should also be studied, that is, policies that decide on rejection or not of a message based on information such as the time the message has spent in the system, the arrival process up to the current time, etc. [12].

Finally, we also mention that the AoI α\alpha defined in (3) may not be the most appropriate measure of freshness as it incorporates information about the arrival process as well. A different measure [10] is β⁡(t)=A⁡(t)−A⁡(D⁡(t))\beta(t)=A(t)-A(D(t)), in the notation of the processes introduced in (1) and (2), the distribution of which may differ significantly from that of α\alpha. Also, it may be interesting to study other performance criteria for AoI-sensitive applications including Cost of Update Delay [14, 6] or message blocking probability.
